implementation_notes: The .NET mechanism is load contexts: create an AssemblyLoadContext(name, isCollectible: true), load the component assembly with LoadFromAssemblyPath(), use an AssemblyDependencyResolver so the component's own dependencies resolve inside its context, instantiate the type that implements the shared IComponent contract and store it in the host's repository. Unload() plus dropping every reference and running a GC cycle actually reclaims the assemblies, which makes this the rare mainstream managed runtime where the pattern's unlink half works; Assembly.LoadFrom/Assembly.LoadFile put the assembly in the default context and can never be unloaded, so they are the classic manual form only when replacement is handled by restarting the process. MEF (System.ComponentModel.Composition) is the framework-level alternative when you want catalog/attribute-driven composition instead of writing the repository yourself.
pitfalls: A collectible context is reclaimed only when nothing references it: static fields, running threads, event handlers, timers and cached Type/MethodInfo objects rooted elsewhere pin the whole component, so Unload() is honoured but memory is never returned.

The contract assembly must be shared rather than duplicated: if the component context loads its own copy of IComponent (or resolves it from a different path), the loaded type implements a different identity and the cast fails - resolve the contract from the default context.

Unload() is cooperative and asynchronous (the context enters Unloading and completes after the finalizer/GC cycle), so nothing may call into the context after the request; queued work and finalizers must be drained first.
